rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: The colligative property used for the determination of molar mass of polymers and proteins is :
rows.solution:
OSMOTIC PRESSURE is used to determine the molar mass of polymers and proteins.

A polymer or protein has an enormous molar mass, so even a substantial mass of it dissolves to give very FEW MOLES — and every colligative property depends on the number of particles. The depression in freezing point would be a few thousandths of a degree, below what a thermometer can read reliably; the elevation in boiling point and the relative lowering of vapour pressure are just as small.

Osmotic pressure is the exception on three counts.

Its MAGNITUDE is large and readily measured even for a very dilute solution, so the tiny number of moles still gives a workable reading.

It is measured at ROOM TEMPERATURE, so the protein is not heated and does not denature — which the boiling point method would risk.

It uses MOLARITY rather than molality, which is the concentration a laboratory can prepare directly.

The other three options are all genuine colligative properties; they are simply too small here to use.

rows.stem: Low concentration of oxygen in the blood and tissues of people living at high altitude is due to :

options.label: D
options.text: both low temperature and high atmospheric pressure

rows.solution:
The cause is LOW ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE.

By HENRY'S LAW the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to its PARTIAL PRESSURE above the liquid:
\(p = \mathrm{K_H}\,x\)

At high altitude the total atmospheric pressure is low, so the partial pressure of oxygen is low with it, and correspondingly less oxygen dissolves in the blood. The resulting shortage in the blood and tissues is called ANOXIA, and it makes climbers weak and unable to think clearly.

Note which quantity does the work. The COMPOSITION of the air is essentially the same at altitude as at sea level — about 21% oxygen either way — so it is not that the air holds less oxygen but that the whole column presses less hard.

Low temperature is the distractor, and it acts the OTHER way: dissolving a gas is exothermic, so cold actually INCREASES solubility. The two options naming high atmospheric pressure have the effect exactly reversed.

rows.stem:
The correct cell to represent the following reaction is :
\(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\)
rows.solution:
The correct representation is \(\mathrm{Zn} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} \parallel \mathrm{Ag^+} \mid \mathrm{Ag}\).

The convention has three parts, and all three must be satisfied.

The ANODE is written on the LEFT and the CATHODE on the RIGHT. In \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{Ag^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\) zinc is OXIDISED, so zinc is the anode; silver ion is REDUCED, so silver is the cathode.

Within each half cell the species are written in the order the electrons flow. At the anode that means metal first, then its ion: \(\mathrm{Zn} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\). At the cathode it means ion first, then metal: \(\mathrm{Ag^+} \mid \mathrm{Ag}\).

The double vertical line \(\parallel\) marks the SALT BRIDGE between them; a single line marks a phase boundary within a half cell.

Each of the other three gets one of these wrong — putting silver on the left, or reversing the order within a half cell, or both.

rows.stem: \(\Delta \mathrm{G}\) and \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}\) for a spontaneous reaction will be :
rows.solution:
For a spontaneous reaction \(\Delta \mathrm{G}\) is NEGATIVE and \(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\) is POSITIVE.

The two are linked by
\(\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = -n\mathrm{F}E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}\)

and both \(n\) and \(\mathrm{F}\) are positive quantities. The MINUS SIGN in that relation is what forces the two signs to be opposite: a positive cell potential necessarily gives a negative free energy change.

A negative \(\Delta \mathrm{G}\) is the thermodynamic condition for spontaneity, and a positive cell potential is the electrical statement of the same thing — a cell that will drive current by itself. The two say one thing in two languages, which is why no option with matching signs can be right.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Which of the following is affected by catalyst ?
rows.solution:
A catalyst affects the ACTIVATION ENERGY, \(E_a\).

A catalyst works by providing an ALTERNATIVE PATH from reactants to products, one with a LOWER energy barrier. A larger fraction of collisions then carries enough energy to cross it, so the rate constant rises and the reaction speeds up.

What a catalyst does NOT change is anything that depends only on the reactants and products themselves. \(\Delta \mathrm{H}\), \(\Delta \mathrm{G}\) and \(\Delta \mathrm{S}\) are all STATE FUNCTIONS: their values depend on where the reaction starts and finishes, not on the route taken between.

Two consequences follow, and both are worth remembering. A catalyst cannot make a non-spontaneous reaction happen, since it leaves \(\Delta \mathrm{G}\) untouched. And it lowers the barrier in BOTH directions equally, so it speeds the forward and backward reactions alike — a catalyst brings an equilibrium on faster without shifting its position.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The order of the reaction
\(\mathrm{H_2\,(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2\,(g)} \xrightarrow{\ h\nu\ } 2\mathrm{HCl\,(g)}\) is :
rows.solution:
The reaction is ZERO ORDER.

The combination of hydrogen and chlorine in light is a photochemical chain reaction. Light initiates it by splitting chlorine molecules into atoms, so the rate is governed by the INTENSITY OF THE LIGHT ABSORBED rather than by how much hydrogen or chlorine is present. A rate that does not depend on the reactant concentrations is zero order by definition:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{H_2}]^0[\mathrm{Cl_2}]^0 = k\)

The reaction over water is the standard textbook example of a zero order reaction, alongside the decomposition of ammonia on a hot platinum surface — where the rate is set instead by how much of the surface is available.

[The marking scheme keys zero, then adds that FULL MARK IS TO BE AWARDED FOR ANY OPTION. Its grounds are not printed; the chemistry above is the reason the keyed answer is the keyed answer.]

rows.stem: The most common and stable oxidation state of a Lanthanoid is :
rows.solution:
The most common and stable oxidation state of a lanthanoid is \(+3\).

The configuration explains it. A lanthanoid atom is \([\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^{n}\,5d^{0\text{ or }1}\,6s^2\), and losing three electrons — the two \(6s\) and one from \(5d\) or \(4f\) — gives an ion that is stable across the whole series.

The \(4f\) electrons that remain are BURIED deep inside the atom, well shielded by the \(5s\) and \(5p\) shells, so they are hardly touched by the chemical environment. That is why every lanthanoid behaves so much like every other, and why they are so hard to separate.

Other states do appear, but only where they reach a specially stable \(4f\) configuration: cerium gives \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\), reaching the empty \(4f^0\), and europium gives \(\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}\), reaching the half-filled \(4f^7\). Both are exceptions, and both revert to \(+3\) readily — which is why europium(II) is a reducing agent and cerium(IV) an oxidising one.

rows.stem: The compounds \(\mathrm{[Co(SO_4)\,(NH_3)_5]\,Br}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(Br)\,(NH_3)_5]\,SO_4}\) represent :
rows.solution:
The pair exhibits IONISATION ISOMERISM.

Ionisation isomers have the same FORMULA but EXCHANGE an ion between the coordination sphere and the position of counter ion. Compare the two: in one the sulphate is the ligand and the bromide the counter ion, and in the other they have swapped places.

The name is earned in solution, because each releases a DIFFERENT ion:
the compound with bromide outside gives a pale yellow precipitate with silver nitrate, free bromide being present;
the compound with sulphate outside gives a white precipitate with barium chloride instead.

Each fails the other's test, which is how the two are told apart — and it is the same reasoning by which Werner established what lies inside a coordination sphere and what lies outside.

The other three would each need something absent here: optical isomerism needs a chiral arrangement, linkage isomerism an ambidentate ligand, and coordination isomerism BOTH ions to be complex.

rows.stem: The synthesis of alkyl fluoride is best obtained from :
rows.solution:
Alkyl fluorides are best obtained by the SWARTZ REACTION.

An alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a metallic fluoride — antimony(III) fluoride, mercury(II) fluoride, cobalt(II) fluoride or silver fluoride — and the halogen is exchanged:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}Br} + \mathrm{AgF} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3{-}F} + \mathrm{AgBr}\)

The indirect route is necessary because DIRECT fluorination is impractical. Fluorine reacts with a hydrocarbon so violently that the carbon skeleton is destroyed rather than substituted, and controlling it is not worth the trouble.

Each other option makes a different halide. The FINKELSTEIN reaction is the close analogue but makes IODIDES, exchanging an alkyl chloride or bromide for iodide with sodium iodide in dry acetone. The SANDMEYER reaction replaces a diazonium group on a RING by chlorine, bromine or cyanide. Free radical halogenation gives a mixture of isomers, and with fluorine it is uncontrollable.

rows.stem: In the reaction \(\mathrm{R-OH} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ZnCl_2}} \mathrm{RCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\), what is the correct order of reactivity of alcohol ?
rows.solution:
The order of reactivity is \(1^{\circ} < 2^{\circ} < 3^{\circ}\).

This is the LUCAS test reaction, and it proceeds by an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) mechanism. Zinc chloride coordinates to the hydroxyl oxygen, converting the poor leaving group \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into a good one; the group then departs, leaving a CARBOCATION, which chloride attacks.

The slow step is forming the carbocation, so the reactivity follows the stability of the cation — and alkyl groups stabilise a positive charge by releasing electron density towards it. A tertiary carbon has three of them, a secondary two, a primary one.

The test is practical because the rates differ so visibly: a TERTIARY alcohol turns cloudy IMMEDIATELY, a SECONDARY one within about five minutes, and a PRIMARY one only on heating.

Note that the order is the REVERSE of an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction's, where crowding round the carbon hinders backside attack.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\) on reaction with NaOH and \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in alcoholic medium gives :
rows.solution:
The product is METHANAMINE, \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\).

This is the HOFMANN BROMAMIDE DEGRADATION, which converts an amide to a primary amine with ONE CARBON FEWER:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The carbon lost is the CARBONYL carbon, which leaves as carbonate, while the methyl group MIGRATES from that carbon to the nitrogen.

Counting carbons disposes of two options at once: ethanamine and bromoethane both have TWO carbons, and no reaction of this kind adds one. Sodium ethanoate would be the product of HYDROLYSIS, which needs alkali and water without the bromine — the bromine is what makes the difference between hydrolysing the amide and degrading it.

rows.stem: Which of the following is least basic ?
rows.solution:
ANILINE is the least basic.

Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen's lone pair is to accept a proton, and aniline's is not available at all — it is DELOCALISED into the benzene ring, spread over the ortho and para carbons by resonance. Committing the pair to the ring means it cannot also be given to a proton.

The three aliphatic species have no such drain. Their lone pairs stay on the nitrogen, and the methyl groups even push further density onto it.

The \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values show how large the gap is: dimethylamine 3.27, trimethylamine 4.22, ammonia 4.75, aniline 9.38 — aniline weaker than the others by about \(10^5\) to \(10^6\).

Note also that this is a comparison the ring wins outright: the small differences among the three aliphatic species, which turn on solvation and crowding, are a much finer question than the one the ring settles.

rows.stem: The glycosidic linkage involved in linking the glucose units in amylase part of starch is :
rows.solution:
The linkage is \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) \(\alpha\).

Starch has two components, and they differ in exactly this respect. AMYLOSE is a LINEAR, water-soluble polymer of \(\alpha\)-glucose in which each unit is joined to the next through a \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) \(\alpha\) glycosidic linkage, and it makes up about 15 to 20% of starch.

AMYLOPECTIN, the rest, is BRANCHED: its chains are also \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) linked, but at the branch points the linkage is \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_6}\).

The \(\alpha\) part matters as much as the numbering. CELLULOSE is also a \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) linked polymer of glucose, but of the \(\beta\) anomer — and that single difference is why we can digest starch and cannot digest cellulose.

[The stem as printed says the "amylase" part of starch, where AMYLOSE is meant; amylase is the enzyme that digests starch. The marking scheme records this as a printing error and directs full marks for any attempt.]

rows.stem: An \(\alpha\)-helix is a structural feature of :
rows.solution:
The \(\alpha\)-helix is a structural feature of POLYPEPTIDES.

It is a SECONDARY structure of proteins: the polypeptide chain coils into a right-handed spiral, and each \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) group hydrogen bonds to the \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) of the residue FOUR places further along the same chain. Those hydrogen bonds run roughly parallel to the axis and hold the coil in shape.

Individually each bond is weak, but there are very many, and together they hold firmly. Their weakness is functional: it lets a protein be DENATURED, unwinding on heating or on a change of pH without any covalent bond breaking.

None of the other options can form one. Sucrose is a single small disaccharide, far too small to coil. Starch does form a helix, but a quite different one, stabilised by its own geometry rather than by backbone hydrogen bonds of this kind. Nucleotides are single units — the DOUBLE helix belongs to the polymer built from them, not to the unit.

The \(\beta\)-pleated sheet is the other secondary structure, with the chains stretched flat and hydrogen bonded to their neighbours.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is o- and p-directing in electrophilic substitution reactions.
Reason (R) : Aniline cannot undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The Assertion is correct. The amino group donates its nitrogen lone pair into the ring, raising the electron density most at the ORTHO and PARA positions, so an electrophile attacks there.

The Reason is also correct. Aniline does NOT undergo the Friedel-Crafts reaction — its nitrogen lone pair makes it a Lewis BASE, so it combines with the aluminium chloride catalyst to form a salt. The catalyst is consumed, and the nitrogen now carries a POSITIVE charge which deactivates the ring.

But the two concern DIFFERENT things. The Assertion is about WHERE an electrophile attacks; the Reason is about ONE REACTION that does not happen at all, and for a quite separate cause — the catalyst, not the directing effect.

Indeed the Reason almost cuts against the Assertion: the reason aniline fails at Friedel-Crafts is that the amino group STOPS behaving as an electron donor in that medium.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Acetylation of aniline gives a monosubstituted product.
Reason (R) : Activating effect of \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH_3}\) group is more than that of amino group.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Acetylation of aniline does give a monosubstituted product — that is precisely why it is done. Bromine water with aniline itself gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline, with no way to stop at one; with acetanilide it gives the para product alone.

But the Reason has the comparison the wrong way round. The activating effect of \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH_3}\) is LESS than that of \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\), not more.

And that reduction is exactly why the trick works. In acetanilide the nitrogen's lone pair is shared with the neighbouring CARBONYL group, which competes with the ring for it. Less density reaches the ring, so the group remains ortho, para directing but is far less activating — enough for one substitution, not for three.

Corrected to "less than", the Reason would have explained the Assertion perfectly. As written it would predict the opposite, since a MORE activating group would give more substitution rather than less.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The molecularity of the reaction \(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HBr}\) appears to be 2.
Reason (R) : Two molecules of the reactants are involved in the given elementary reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

MOLECULARITY counts the species that must COLLIDE SIMULTANEOUSLY in a single elementary step. The equation \(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HBr}\) shows two molecules on the left, so if the reaction were elementary its molecularity would be 2 — and the Reason states exactly that.

Note the word APPEARS, which the Assertion uses carefully. Molecularity is read off an equation only when the equation describes a real single step, and the formation of hydrogen bromide is in fact a chain reaction going through several steps. Its measured ORDER comes out as 1.5, which is the evidence: a fractional order cannot belong to a single elementary step.

So the Assertion claims only what can be read from the equation as written, and the Reason gives precisely the ground for reading it that way.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Low spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed.
Reason (R) : Crystal field splitting energy is less than pairing energy for tetrahedral complexes.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Low spin tetrahedral complexes ARE rare, almost to the point of never being seen — and the Reason names the cause.

A tetrahedral field splits the d orbitals only weakly, for two reasons: there are only FOUR ligands rather than six, and none of them points DIRECTLY at a d orbital, the ligands approaching between the axes rather than along them. The result is
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}} = \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\)

for the same metal and ligands.

That figure is essentially always SMALLER than the pairing energy. With \(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}} < \mathrm{P}\), promoting an electron to the upper set costs less than pairing it in the lower, so the electrons spread out and the complex is HIGH SPIN.

A low spin tetrahedral complex would need a ligand field strong enough to overcome the pairing energy despite that four-ninths handicap, and no ordinary ligand manages it.

rows.stem: What is Henry's law ? Give one application of it.
rows.solution:
HENRY'S LAW states that the PARTIAL PRESSURE of a gas in the vapour phase is directly PROPORTIONAL to the MOLE FRACTION of that gas dissolved in the solution:
\(p = \mathrm{K_H}\,x\)

Here \(p\) is the partial pressure of the gas above the solution, \(x\) its mole fraction in solution, and \(\mathrm{K_H}\) the Henry's law constant, whose value depends on the gas, the solvent and the TEMPERATURE.

A HIGHER \(\mathrm{K_H}\) means a LOWER solubility, since a greater pressure is then needed to dissolve the same amount. And because dissolving a gas is exothermic, \(\mathrm{K_H}\) increases with temperature — gases are less soluble in warm liquids.

AN APPLICATION: soft drinks and soda water are SEALED UNDER HIGH PRESSURE of carbon dioxide, so that a large amount dissolves. Opening the bottle drops the pressure and the excess gas fizzes out.

Two other applications are worth knowing. Deep-sea divers breathe oxygen diluted with HELIUM rather than nitrogen, because helium is far less soluble in blood and so does not come out of solution as bubbles on ascent — the painful condition called the bends. And at high altitude the low partial pressure of oxygen means less dissolves in the blood, causing anoxia.

rows.stem: On diluting two electrolytes 'A' and 'B', the \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) of 'A' increases 25 times while that of 'B' increases by \(1{\cdot}5\) times. Which of the two electrolytes is strong ? Justify your answer graphically.
rows.solution:
'B' IS THE STRONG ELECTROLYTE.

The SIZE of the rise on dilution is what separates them, and the two have different causes.

A STRONG electrolyte is already COMPLETELY DISSOCIATED at every concentration, so dilution cannot produce any new ions. Its molar conductivity rises only SLIGHTLY, and only because the ions move further apart and interfere with one another's migration less. A rise of 1.5 times is exactly that modest increase — so 'B' is the strong electrolyte.

A WEAK electrolyte is only partly ionised, and dilution shifts that equilibrium towards MORE ions, so one mole of it furnishes many more. Its molar conductivity therefore rises STEEPLY. A rise of 25 times can only be this, so 'A' is the weak electrolyte.

GRAPHICALLY, plotting \(\Lambda_m\) against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\):

'B' gives a NEARLY STRAIGHT LINE of gentle slope, which meets the vertical axis at a definite intercept — and extrapolating to that intercept is the standard way of finding \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for a strong electrolyte.

'A' gives a CURVE that rises steeply as the concentration approaches zero, running almost parallel to the vertical axis and never meeting it. No intercept can be read, so the limiting value for a weak electrolyte must be obtained from KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW instead.

rows.stem: The electrical resistance of a column of \(0{\cdot}05\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) NaOH solution of diameter 1 cm and length 50 cm is \(5{\cdot}55 \times 10^{3}\) ohm. Calculate the conductivity.
rows.solution:
The column of solution is a cylinder, so find its cross-sectional area from the diameter. The radius is 0.5 cm:
\(\mathrm{A} = \pi r^2 = 3{\cdot}14 \times (0{\cdot}5)^2 = 0{\cdot}785\ \mathrm{cm^2}\), and \(l = 50\) cm

Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistance multiplied by the cell constant \(l/\mathrm{A}\):
\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\left(\dfrac{l}{\mathrm{A}}\right) = \dfrac{l}{\mathrm{R} \times \mathrm{A}}\)
\(= \dfrac{50}{0{\cdot}785 \times 5{\cdot}55 \times 10^{3}}\)

\(\kappa = 11{\cdot}47 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

The DIAMETER is the trap: it must be halved before squaring, and using 1 cm as the radius would make the area four times too large and the answer four times too small.

Note that the concentration is not needed here. It would be needed for the MOLAR conductivity, \(\Lambda_m = \kappa \times 1000/\mathrm{C}\), which is a different quantity.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete the following equations :
(a) \(2\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 5\mathrm{NO_2^{-}} + 6\mathrm{H}^{+} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H}^{+} + 6\mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
(a) Permanganate oxidises nitrite to nitrate in acidic medium:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{NO_2^-} + 6\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{NO_3^-} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Ten electrons change hands. Manganese falls from \(+7\) to \(+2\), five electrons each for two atoms; nitrogen rises from \(+3\) to \(+5\), two electrons each for five atoms. The purple solution is decolourised, which is what makes permanganate its own indicator in a titration.

(b) Dichromate is reduced to chromium(III), the six electrons being supplied by whatever is being oxidised:
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6e^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Each of the two chromium atoms falls from \(+6\) to \(+3\), three electrons apiece. The orange solution turns green.

Check the balance both ways in each case: the ATOMS must match, and so must the CHARGE. In the second half-equation the left side carries \(-2 + 14 - 6 = +6\) and the right \(2 \times (+3) = +6\), which confirms the number of electrons.

rows.stem:
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCl_5}} \text{'A'} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{AgCN}} \text{'B'}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\text{ethanol}} \text{'A'} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HBr}} \text{'B'}\)
Identify 'A' and 'B' in the above reactions.
rows.solution:
(a) Phosphorus pentachloride replaces the hydroxyl group of the alcohol by chlorine:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CHClCH_3}\), 2-chloropropane

Silver cyanide then substitutes for the chloride — and the product is the ISOCYANIDE, not the cyanide:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH(NC)CH_3}\), 2-isocyanopropane

Which atom attacks depends on the metal. Silver cyanide is largely COVALENT, so only its NITROGEN lone pair is free and the nitrogen attacks. Potassium cyanide is ionic, the cyanide ion attacks through its CARBON, and the product would have been the nitrile.

(b) Alcoholic potassium hydroxide supplies alkoxide ions, which are strong BASES and cause ELIMINATION:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2}\), propene

Adding hydrogen bromide then follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE, the bromine going to the carbon that gives the more stable, secondary carbocation:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CHBrCH_3}\), 2-bromopropane

Note that the pair of steps has MOVED the halogen from carbon 1 to carbon 2 — which is the standard way of shifting a substituent along a chain.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Phenol is a stronger acid than an alcohol.
(ii) The boiling point of alcohols decreases with increase in branching of alkyl chain.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the PHENOXIDE ION is stabilised by RESONANCE and an alkoxide ion is not.

Acidity is decided by the stability of the anion left behind. When phenol loses its proton, the negative charge on the oxygen is DELOCALISED into the benzene ring, spreading to the ortho and para carbons, so it is not concentrated on one atom.

An alcohol has no such relief. Its alkoxide ion keeps the whole charge on the oxygen, and the alkyl group even pushes further density towards it, making matters worse.

There is a second contribution: phenol's carbon-bearing-oxygen is \(sp^2\) and so more electronegative than an alcohol's \(sp^3\) carbon, which helps draw density away from the oxygen even before the proton leaves.

The difference is large — phenol \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) 10, ethanol about 16 — which is why phenol dissolves in sodium hydroxide and an alcohol does not.

(ii) Because BRANCHING reduces the SURFACE AREA of the molecule.

Boiling requires the intermolecular forces to be overcome, and among isomeric alcohols the hydrogen bonding is much the same — each has one \(\mathrm{O-H}\) group. What differs is the VAN DER WAALS attraction, and that depends on how much surface two molecules can present to each other.

A straight chain is extended and can lie alongside its neighbour over its whole length. A branched isomer is compact, tending towards a sphere, and a sphere has the least surface for a given volume. Less contact means weaker attraction and a lower boiling point.

Butan-1-ol boils at 391 K, while its most branched isomer, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, boils at 356 K.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[443\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H}^{+}} \mathrm{CH_2 = CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
(ii) Write the equation involved in Reimer-Tiemann reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) MECHANISM OF DEHYDRATION AT 443 K, in three steps.

STEP 1 — protonation of the alcohol. The oxygen uses a lone pair to pick up a proton. This step is FAST and reversible, and its purpose is to turn the poor leaving group \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into the good one, water:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\ddot{O}H} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

STEP 2 — loss of water to give the CARBOCATION. This is the SLOW, rate determining step, since a bond breaks and a charged species is created:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}\overset{+}{O}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

STEP 3 — elimination of a proton from the carbon next to the positive centre; the pair of electrons left behind forms the double bond, and the catalyst is regenerated:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The TEMPERATURE selects the product. At 413 K a second alcohol molecule attacks the protonated one instead, and the product is ethoxyethane; only at 443 K does elimination win.

(ii) REIMER-TIEMANN REACTION. Phenol with chloroform and aqueous alkali, followed by acidification, gives an aldehyde group at the ORTHO position:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{o\text{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} + 3\mathrm{NaCl} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is SALICYLALDEHYDE, 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde. The attacking species is DICHLOROCARBENE, generated when the alkali removes chloroform's hydrogen, and the intermediate is the substituted benzal chloride, which the alkali hydrolyses to the aldehyde.

rows.stem:
Explain briefly :
(a) Carbylamine reaction
(b) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
rows.solution:
(a) CARBYLAMINE REACTION. A PRIMARY amine, aliphatic or aromatic, heated with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide gives an ISOCYANIDE — a carbylamine — recognised at once by its exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R{-}NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

It is a TEST for primary amines, and a highly specific one: forming the isocyanide requires the nitrogen to give up BOTH of its hydrogens, so secondary and tertiary amines do not respond at all.

The attacking species is dichlorocarbene, generated from the chloroform by the alkali — the same intermediate as in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction.

(b) GABRIEL PHTHALIMIDE SYNTHESIS, in three steps:
\(\text{phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}} \text{potassium phthalimide} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{R{-}X}} \text{N-alkylphthalimide} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{R{-}NH_2} + \text{sodium phthalate}\)

Potassium hydroxide removes the imide's \(\mathrm{N-H}\) hydrogen, which is acidic because of the two flanking carbonyl groups. The anion then displaces halide from an alkyl halide in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) step, and alkaline hydrolysis finally frees the amine.

Its value is that the product is a PURE PRIMARY amine: the nitrogen is locked into the ring and cannot be alkylated twice, so no secondary or tertiary amine contaminates it — the failing of ammonolysis. It does NOT work for aromatic amines, since an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution.

rows.stem:
(a) Write chemical reaction to show that open structure of D-glucose contains the straight chain.
(b) What type of linkage is responsible for the formation of protein ?
rows.solution:
(a) Heating glucose with HYDROIODIC ACID and red phosphorus strips out every oxygen and gives N-HEXANE:
\(\mathrm{CHO{-}(CHOH)_4{-}CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{HI}} \mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_3}\)

The product is what proves the point. Hexane is a STRAIGHT chain of six carbons, and since the reduction removes only the oxygens and leaves the carbon skeleton untouched, glucose's six carbons must likewise be joined in an UNBRANCHED chain.

This was one of the first structural facts established about glucose, and it narrowed the possibilities enormously before the position of the carbonyl group was settled by other tests.

(b) The PEPTIDE LINKAGE is responsible for forming proteins.

It is the amide bond \(-\mathrm{CO{-}NH}-\), formed when the carboxyl group of one amino acid condenses with the amino group of the next and a molecule of water is lost:
\(\mathrm{H_2N{-}CHR{-}COOH} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}CHR'{-}COOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2N{-}CHR{-}CO{-}NH{-}CHR'{-}COOH} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

A chain of \(n\) amino acids therefore contains \(n - 1\) peptide bonds, and it is that sequence that constitutes the protein's PRIMARY structure.

rows.stem:
(a) Differentiate between Ideal solution and Non-ideal solution.
(b) 30 g of urea is dissolved in 846 g of water. Calculate the vapour pressure of water for this solution if vapour pressure of pure water at 298 K is \(23{\cdot}8\) mm Hg.
rows.solution:
(a) Differences between an ideal and a non-ideal solution.

An IDEAL solution OBEYS RAOULT'S LAW at all concentrations and all temperatures; a NON-IDEAL solution does not, showing either a positive or a negative deviation from it.

For an ideal solution \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}\mathrm{V} = 0\) and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}\mathrm{H} = 0\) — mixing changes neither the volume nor the enthalpy. For a non-ideal solution both are non-zero.

The molecular reason lies behind both statements. An ideal solution forms when the interactions between UNLIKE molecules are essentially the SAME as those between like ones, so a molecule cannot tell what surrounds it. Benzene with toluene, and hexane with heptane, are close to ideal for exactly that reason. Where the unlike interaction is stronger or weaker, the deviation follows.

(b) Raoult's law gives the relative lowering of vapour pressure as the mole fraction of the solute. Urea is 60 g per mole and water 18:
\(n_{\text{urea}} = \dfrac{30}{60} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(n_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{846}{18} = 47\ \mathrm{mol}\)

\(\dfrac{p^{\circ}_{\mathrm{A}} - p_{\mathrm{A}}}{p^{\circ}_{\mathrm{A}}} = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{B}}}{n_{\mathrm{A}} + n_{\mathrm{B}}} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}5}{47{\cdot}5} = 0{\cdot}01053\)

\(p_{\mathrm{A}} = 23{\cdot}8 \times (1 - 0{\cdot}01053)\)

\(p_{\mathrm{A}} = 23{\cdot}55\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

The dilute approximation \(n_{\mathrm{B}}/n_{\mathrm{A}} = 0{\cdot}5/47\) gives the same answer to three figures, and the marking scheme accepts either route.

The check is that the vapour pressure must be slightly BELOW the pure solvent's 23.8, since a non-volatile solute can only lower it.

rows.stem:
Write main product formed when :
(a) Methyl chloride is treated with NaI/Acetone.
(b) 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is subjected to hydrolysis.
(c) n-Butyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH.
rows.solution:
(a) Sodium iodide in DRY ACETONE exchanges the halogen — the FINKELSTEIN reaction:
\(\mathrm{CH_3Cl} + \mathrm{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{NaCl}\)

The product is IODOMETHANE, and the SOLVENT is what drives it: sodium iodide dissolves in acetone while sodium chloride does not, so the chloride precipitates out and pulls the equilibrium across.

(b) 2,4,6-TRINITROPHENOL, picric acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3Cl} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{warm}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

An aryl halide is normally inert to nucleophilic substitution, and chlorobenzene itself needs 623 K and 300 atmospheres. Here the THREE NITRO GROUPS change everything: being strongly electron-withdrawing, and sitting ortho and para to the chlorine, they stabilise the negative intermediate formed when the nucleophile attacks. Warm water alone is then enough.

(c) Alcoholic potassium hydroxide supplies alkoxide ions, strong bases that cause ELIMINATION:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{alc. }\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is BUT-1-ENE. Only one alkene is possible, since the \(\beta\) carbon is at the end of the chain. AQUEOUS potassium hydroxide would have substituted instead, giving butan-1-ol.

rows.stem:
How do you convert the following : (Any three)
(a) Phenol to picric acid
(b) Propanone to 2-Methylpropan-2-ol
(c) Phenol to anisole
(d) Propene to Propan-1-ol
rows.solution:
(a) PHENOL TO PICRIC ACID. Concentrated nitric acid nitrates phenol at all three activated positions, the hydroxyl being strongly ortho, para directing:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{HNO_3} \xrightarrow{\text{conc.}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The product is 2,4,6-TRINITROPHENOL. In practice phenol is first sulphonated with concentrated sulphuric acid and then nitrated, which avoids the heavy oxidation that direct nitration causes.

(b) PROPANONE TO 2-METHYLPROPAN-2-OL. A Grignard reagent adds a methyl group to the carbonyl carbon, and a KETONE gives a TERTIARY alcohol:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}OH}\)

(c) PHENOL TO ANISOLE — the WILLIAMSON synthesis:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5ONa} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3I}} \mathrm{C_6H_5{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{NaI}\)

The order matters: the phenoxide must be the NUCLEOPHILE and the methyl iodide the substrate. The reverse combination — an aryl halide with methoxide — gives nothing, since an aryl carbon is not open to substitution.

(d) PROPENE TO PROPAN-1-OL. The hydroxyl must go to the TERMINAL carbon, which is ANTI-MARKOVNIKOV, so hydroboration-oxidation is required:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} (\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O_2}/\mathrm{OH^-}} 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH}\)

Acid-catalysed hydration would have given propan-2-ol instead.

rows.stem:
Explain why :
(i) Carboxyl group in benzoic acid is meta directing.
(ii) Sodium bisulphite is used for the purification of aldehydes and ketones.
(iii) Carboxylic acids do not give characteristic reactions of carbonyl group.
rows.solution:
(i) Because the carboxyl group WITHDRAWS electron density, and the meta position is the one it deactivates LEAST.

The \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group pulls density out of the ring both inductively and by resonance, so benzoic acid is DEACTIVATED overall and substitutes more slowly than benzene.

Where the attack goes is settled by comparing the three intermediates. Attacking at the ORTHO or PARA position gives a carbocation with the positive charge on the very carbon bearing the electron-withdrawing group — two positive centres side by side, which is strongly destabilising. Attacking at META avoids that coincidence entirely.

So the meta intermediate is the LEAST unstable of the three, and substitution goes there. The direction comes from a comparison of shortfalls, not from any increase in density.

(ii) Because the BISULPHITE ADDUCT is a CRYSTALLINE SOLID that can be separated and then reversed.

An aldehyde, and a ketone with a small alkyl group, adds sodium bisulphite to give a white crystalline addition product:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} + \mathrm{NaHSO_3} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C(OH)(SO_3Na)}\)

The crystals are filtered off, leaving the impurities behind in solution. Warming them with dilute acid or alkali REVERSES the addition and returns the pure carbonyl compound.

The reaction's SELECTIVITY is what makes it work: the adduct forms readily with aldehydes and methyl ketones, and not with bulkier ketones, so the method separates one kind of carbonyl compound from another as well as from non-carbonyl impurities.

(iii) Because the carboxyl carbon is stabilised by RESONANCE with the hydroxyl oxygen.

That oxygen donates a lone pair into the carbonyl group, so resonance structures can be drawn placing a negative charge on the carbonyl oxygen and a positive one on the hydroxyl oxygen — with the carbon between them relieved of much of its deficiency. In effect the carbon LOSES its carbonyl character.

An aldehyde or ketone has no such donor beside it, only hydrogen or alkyl groups, which cannot supply a lone pair, so its carbon stays strongly electrophilic.

The consequence is that carboxylic acids give none of the characteristic additions: no bisulphite adduct, no cyanohydrin, no condensation with ammonia derivatives.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: An organic compound 'A', having the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) on treatment with Cu at 573 K, gives 'B'. 'B' does not reduce Fehling's solution but gives a yellow precipitate of the compound 'C' with \(\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}\). Deduce the structures of A, B and C.
rows.solution:
Take the clues in order.

'A' has the formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) — a saturated three-carbon alcohol, so either propan-1-ol or propan-2-ol. COPPER AT 573 K dehydrogenates an alcohol, and which product it gives depends on which alcohol it was: a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde, a secondary alcohol a ketone.

'B' does NOT reduce Fehling's solution, so it is not an aldehyde — it is a KETONE, and 'A' must therefore be the SECONDARY alcohol:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}\), propan-2-ol
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), propanone
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{Cu}} \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} + \mathrm{H_2}\)

'B' gives a yellow precipitate with iodine and alkali, which confirms the \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group that propanone has:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CHI_3}\), iodoform
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CHI_3}\downarrow + \mathrm{CH_3COONa} + 3\mathrm{NaI} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The two tests work TOGETHER here: the negative Fehling result rules out the aldehyde, and the positive iodoform result confirms the methyl ketone. Either alone would have left the answer open.

rows.stem:
(a) What are the hydrolysis products of (i) Lactose, (ii) Maltose ?
(b) Give the basic structural difference between starch and cellulose.
rows.solution:
(a)(i) LACTOSE hydrolyses to GLUCOSE and GALACTOSE.

It is the sugar of milk, a disaccharide of one \(\beta\)-galactose unit and one glucose unit. Because the glucose unit keeps a free anomeric carbon and can still open into its aldehyde form, lactose is a REDUCING sugar.

(ii) MALTOSE hydrolyses to TWO MOLECULES OF GLUCOSE.

It is built from two \(\alpha\)-glucose units joined \(\mathrm{C_1}\) to \(\mathrm{C_4}\), and it too is a reducing sugar for the same reason. It is the unit from which starch is built, and it is obtained when starch is partly hydrolysed.

(b) The basic structural difference is the ANOMER from which each is built.

STARCH is a polymer of \(\alpha\)-GLUCOSE. Its amylose component is a linear \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_4}\) linked chain; its amylopectin component is branched, with \(\mathrm{C_1}\)-\(\mathrm{C_6}\) linkages at the branch points.

CELLULOSE is a polymer of \(\beta\)-GLUCOSE, linked \(\mathrm{C_1}\) to \(\mathrm{C_4}\) and entirely UNBRANCHED.

The consequence is large. The \(\alpha\) linkage lets the chain COIL, and human enzymes can hydrolyse it. The \(\beta\) linkage gives a STRAIGHT chain that packs into rigid fibres held by hydrogen bonds — strong enough to be the structural material of plants, and indigestible to us.

rows.stem: What is average rate of reaction ?
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
The AVERAGE RATE OF REACTION is the change in the concentration of a reactant or product divided by the TIME INTERVAL over which that change is measured:
\(r_{\mathrm{av}} = -\dfrac{\Delta[\text{Reactant}]}{\Delta t} = +\dfrac{\Delta[\text{Product}]}{\Delta t}\)

The MINUS sign for the reactant makes the rate come out positive, since a reactant's concentration falls and \(\Delta[\mathrm{R}]\) is negative.

The word AVERAGE matters. It is the rate over a FINITE interval, so it reports the mean behaviour across that stretch rather than the rate at any one moment. Since a reaction generally slows as its reactants are consumed, the average over a long interval can differ considerably from the rate at either end of it.

The INSTANTANEOUS rate is the limit as the interval shrinks to zero, \(-d[\mathrm{R}]/dt\), and is found as the slope of the tangent to a concentration-time curve.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Write two factors that affect the rate of reaction.
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
Two factors that affect the rate of a reaction, from among the following.

CONCENTRATION of the reactants. More molecules per unit volume means more collisions per second, so the rate rises. Exactly how steeply is what the ORDER of the reaction measures — and for a zero order reaction it does not rise at all.

TEMPERATURE. Raising it increases both the number of collisions and, far more importantly, the FRACTION of them energetic enough to cross the activation barrier. Near room temperature a rise of ten degrees roughly DOUBLES the rate.

A CATALYST provides an alternative path of lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed.

SURFACE AREA matters where a reactant is a solid: a powder reacts far faster than a lump, because reaction happens only at the surface.

The NATURE OF THE REACTANTS underlies all of these, since it sets how high the barrier is in the first place — which is why an ionic reaction in solution is essentially instantaneous while a covalent one may take hours.

rows.stem:
(1) What happens to rate of reaction for zero order reaction ?
(2) What is the unit of k for zero order reaction ?
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
(1) The rate of a zero order reaction REMAINS CONSTANT throughout — it does not change as the reactants are consumed.
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\)

Since the concentration term vanishes, the rate simply IS the rate constant. A plot of concentration against time is therefore a STRAIGHT LINE of slope \(-k\), not the curve a first order reaction gives.

Such behaviour arises where something other than concentration limits the reaction — the SURFACE of a catalyst, as in the decomposition of ammonia on hot platinum, or the INTENSITY OF LIGHT in a photochemical reaction. The reactant is in such excess that the limiting factor is saturated and stays saturated.

(2) The unit of \(k\) for a zero order reaction is \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

It is the same as the unit of the RATE, and necessarily so: with no concentration term in the rate law, the constant and the rate are the same quantity. This is the only order for which the two units agree.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
(1) For a reaction \(\mathrm{P} + 2\mathrm{Q} \longrightarrow \text{Products}\)
Rate \(= \mathrm{k[P]}^{1/2}\,\mathrm{[Q]}^{1}\). What is the order of the reaction ?
(2) Define pseudo first order reaction with an example.
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
(1) The ORDER is the sum of the exponents in the rate law:
\(\text{Order} = \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 = 1{\cdot}5\)

A FRACTIONAL order is perfectly possible, because order is MEASURED rather than deduced. Note that the coefficients in the equation are 1 and 2, and neither appears in the rate law — the coefficients would have predicted an order of 3.

A fractional order is in fact EVIDENCE that the reaction is complex, going through a sequence of steps rather than a single collision.

(2) A PSEUDO FIRST ORDER reaction is one that is not genuinely first order but BEHAVES as though it were, because one reactant is present in such LARGE EXCESS that its concentration does not measurably change.

That constant concentration can be absorbed into the rate constant:
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}] = k'[\mathrm{A}]\) where \(k' = k[\mathrm{B}]\)

EXAMPLE: the ACID HYDROLYSIS OF AN ESTER in dilute solution:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOC_2H_5} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)

Water is both reactant and solvent, so it is vastly in excess. The reaction is second order in principle and first order in practice. The inversion of cane sugar is the other standard example.

rows.stem: If \(\mathrm{PtCl_2 \cdot 2NH_3}\) does not react with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), what will be its formula ?
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
The formula is \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\).

Only a chloride OUTSIDE the coordination sphere is free in solution, and only a free chloride gives a precipitate with silver nitrate. The compound gives NO precipitate, so NEITHER chloride is outside — both must be LIGANDS, bonded directly to the platinum.

The two ammonia molecules are ligands too, so the coordination number is 4 and the complex is NEUTRAL, with platinum in the \(+2\) state. There is no counter ion at all, which is why nothing ionises.

This is exactly the reasoning Werner used. Comparing how many moles of silver chloride each of a series of compounds precipitated told him how many chlorides lay outside the sphere, and the rest of the formula had then to be accounted for inside it.

The compound is worth knowing for another reason: its CIS isomer is cisplatin, used in cancer chemotherapy.

rows.stem: What is the secondary valency of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) ?
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
The SECONDARY VALENCY is 6.

Werner's secondary valency is what we now call the COORDINATION NUMBER — the number of DONOR ATOMS bonded directly to the metal.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is BIDENTATE: each molecule binds through BOTH of its nitrogens, closing a five-membered chelate ring. Three such ligands therefore supply \(3 \times 2 = 6\) donor atoms, and the geometry is octahedral.

Counting the LIGANDS rather than the donor ATOMS would give 3, and that is the trap the question sets. Secondary valency counts the bonds to the metal, not the molecules supplying them.

The PRIMARY valency is 3, matching cobalt's \(+3\) oxidation state and satisfied by whatever counter ions lie outside.

rows.stem:
(1) Write the formula of Iron(III)hexacyanidoferrate(II).
(2) Write the IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]\,Cl_2}\).
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
(1) IRON(III) HEXACYANIDOFERRATE(II).

Build it from the two halves. The complex anion is \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\): iron is \(+2\), as the bracket after "ferrate" says, and six cyanides give \(-6\). The cation is \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), as the first bracket says.

Balancing the charges requires four cations to three anions — \(4 \times (+3) = +12\) against \(3 \times (-4) = -12\):
\(\mathrm{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3}\)

This is PRUSSIAN BLUE, the intense blue precipitate formed when iron(III) meets hexacyanidoferrate(II), and it is the basis of the standard test for iron(III).

(2) The five ammine ligands are neutral, the chlorido ligand gives \(-1\), and two chlorides sit outside — so cobalt must be \(+3\). Ligands are named in alphabetical order and the counter ion last:
PENTAAMMINECHLORIDOCOBALT(III) CHLORIDE

rows.stem:
Write the hybridization and magnetic behaviour of \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\).
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
Nickel is atomic number 28, and four cyanides give \(-4\) against an overall \(-2\), so nickel is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\).

CYANIDE is a STRONG FIELD ligand. It forces those eight electrons into FOUR of the five d orbitals as four pairs, which leaves ONE inner \(3d\) orbital empty.

That vacant orbital, with the \(4s\) and two of the \(4p\), gives the hybridisation:
HYBRIDISATION: \(dsp^2\), and the shape is SQUARE PLANAR

With every electron paired there is no unpaired spin left:
MAGNETIC BEHAVIOUR: DIAMAGNETIC, \(\mu = 0\)

The contrast with \(\mathrm{[NiCl_4]^{2-}}\) makes the point. Chloride is a weak field ligand and cannot force pairing, so two electrons remain unpaired, no \(3d\) orbital is freed, and that complex is \(sp^3\), tetrahedral and paramagnetic — same metal, same oxidation state, opposite answers on every count.

rows.stem:
(i) State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions. Write an expression for the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid according to Kohlrausch's law.
(ii) Calculate the maximum work and \(\log \mathrm{K_c}\) for the given reaction at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Ni\,(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\,\mathrm{(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\,\mathrm{(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag\,(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}} = -\,0{\cdot}25\) V, \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +\,0{\cdot}80\) V
1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)
rows.solution:
(i) KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW OF INDEPENDENT MIGRATION OF IONS states that the LIMITING molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the SUM of the individual contributions of its cation and its anion, each counted as often as the formula unit provides it:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \nu_+\lambda_+^{\circ} + \nu_-\lambda_-^{\circ}\)

At infinite dilution the ions are so far apart that each moves entirely INDEPENDENTLY of the other, which is what makes the simple sum valid.

FOR ACETIC ACID, which gives one hydrogen ion and one acetate ion:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{H^+}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COO^-})\)

In practice the individual ionic values are obtained from STRONG electrolytes, whose graphs do extrapolate, and combined:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) + \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{HCl}) - \Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{NaCl})\)

The sodium and chloride terms cancel, leaving exactly the hydrogen and acetate contributions. This indirect route is necessary because acetic acid is WEAK, and its own curve never meets the axis.

(ii) The cell potential comes from the two electrode potentials:
\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}80 - (-0{\cdot}25) = 1{\cdot}05\ \mathrm{V}\)

The reaction transfers TWO electrons, so \(n = 2\). The MAXIMUM WORK obtainable is the free energy released, with the sign reversed:
\(W_{\max} = -\Delta_r \mathrm{G}^{\circ} = n\mathrm{F}E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = 2 \times 96500 \times 1{\cdot}05\)

\(W_{\max} = 202650\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(202{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

The equilibrium constant follows from the same potential:
\(\log \mathrm{K_C} = \dfrac{n\,E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}}}{0{\cdot}059} = \dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}05}{0{\cdot}059}\)

\(\log \mathrm{K_C} = 35{\cdot}6\)

Both answers say the same thing: a large positive maximum work and an enormous equilibrium constant, around \(10^{35{\cdot}6}\), mean the reaction goes essentially to completion.

rows.stem:
(i) State Faraday's first law of electrolysis. How much charge, in terms of Faraday, is required for the reduction of 1 mol \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) to Cu ?
(ii) Calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K for
\(\mathrm{Mg\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\,(0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Cu\,(s)}\)
[\(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = +\,2{\cdot}71\) V, 1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(\log 10 = 1\)]
rows.solution:
(i) FARADAY'S FIRST LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS states that the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to the QUANTITY OF ELECTRICITY passed through the electrolyte:
\(w \propto \mathrm{Q}\), that is \(w = \mathrm{Z}\,\mathrm{Q} = \mathrm{Z}\,\mathrm{I}\,t\)

The constant \(\mathrm{Z}\) is the electrochemical equivalent of the substance, the mass deposited by one coulomb.

THE CHARGE FOR ONE MOLE OF COPPER: count the electrons the reduction needs.
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu}\)

Each ion takes TWO electrons, so one mole of copper needs two moles of electrons — 2 FARADAYS, about 193000 coulombs.

(ii) Read the cell diagram: magnesium is on the LEFT and so is the anode; copper ions are reduced at the right. The reaction is \(\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} + \mathrm{Cu}\), so \(n = 2\), and the solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 2{\cdot}71 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{0{\cdot}01} = 2{\cdot}71 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log 10\)
\(= 2{\cdot}71 - 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 2{\cdot}68\ \mathrm{V}\)

The direction of the shift is the check. The PRODUCT ion is ten times more concentrated than the reactant ion, which opposes the forward reaction by Le Chatelier's principle — so the measured emf must come out slightly BELOW the standard value, as it does.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assign reason for each of the following :
(i) Manganese exhibits the highest oxidation state of +7 among the 3d series of transition elements.
(ii) Transition metals and their compounds are generally found to be good catalysts in chemical reactions.
(iii) \(\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}\) is reducing in nature while with the same d-orbital configuration \((\mathrm{d}^{4})\) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}\) is an oxidising agent.
(iv) Zn has lowest enthalpy of atomization.
(v) \(\mathrm{Cu}^{+}\) is unstable in an aqueous solution.
rows.solution:
(i) Because manganese has SEVEN electrons available for bonding, more than any other element of the series.

Manganese is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2\). The highest oxidation state a transition metal reaches is the sum of its \(ns\) electrons and its UNPAIRED \((n-1)d\) electrons, and manganese has FIVE unpaired \(3d\) electrons plus TWO \(4s\) — seven in all, every one of them available.

From iron onwards the \(3d\) electrons begin to PAIR UP, and a paired electron is much less readily used, so the range of states narrows again. Chromium comes closest with \(5 + 1 = 6\), reached in the dichromate ion.

The \(+7\) state survives only in combination with OXYGEN, in the permanganate ion, since only a small and strongly electronegative partner can hold so highly charged a centre.

(ii) Because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form INTERMEDIATE compounds.

A catalyst works by offering a path of lower activation energy, and a transition metal does so by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another — changing oxidation state as it goes, then returning to its original state so that it is not consumed. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process cycles between \(+5\) and \(+4\) in exactly this way.

Finely divided transition metals also provide a large SURFACE on which reactant molecules are adsorbed and held close together with their bonds weakened, as iron does in the Haber process.

(iii) Because the two move in OPPOSITE directions from \(d^4\) towards the stable \(d^5\).

Both ions are \(3d^4\), but what each must do to reach \(3d^5\) differs.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) reaches it by LOSING an electron, becoming \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) — which in an octahedral aqueous environment is the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement. Giving up an electron readily is what a REDUCING agent does, and \(E^{\circ}\) is \(-0{\cdot}41\) V.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) reaches stability by GAINING an electron, becoming \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is the half-filled \(3d^5\). Taking up an electron readily is what an OXIDISING agent does, and \(E^{\circ}\) is \(+1{\cdot}57\) V.

The same configuration therefore gives opposite behaviour, because what counts is not where the ion IS but where it is heading.

(iv) Because zinc has a COMPLETELY FILLED \(3d\) subshell, so its d electrons take no part in metallic bonding.

The enthalpy of atomisation measures the strength of the bond holding the lattice together, and across the series that bond is strengthened by every UNPAIRED d electron contributed to it. Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\) — every d electron paired and held tightly to its own atom — so only the two \(4s\) electrons are available.

With the weakest metallic bond in the series, zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation and the lowest melting and boiling points.

(v) Because \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) DISPROPORTIONATES in water:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

The driving force is HYDRATION ENERGY. The \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ion is smaller and doubly charged, so water binds to it far more strongly than to \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\) — enough to more than pay for the second ionisation energy.

The instability belongs to the AQUEOUS SOLUTION, not to the ion as such. In the SOLID state, with no water to hydrate anything, copper(I) chloride and copper(I) iodide are perfectly stable.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Carry out the following conversions :
(1) Ethanal to But-2-en-1-al
(2) Propanoic acid to 2-chloropropanoic acid
(ii) An alkene with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\) on ozonolysis gives a mixture of two compounds 'B' and 'C'. Compound 'B' gives positive Fehling test and also reacts with iodine and NaOH solution. Compound 'C' does not give Fehling solution test but forms iodoform. Identify the compounds 'A', 'B' and 'C'.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) ETHANAL TO BUT-2-EN-1-AL — count the carbons: TWO in, FOUR out, so two molecules must be joined. This is the ALDOL CONDENSATION:
\(2\,\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CH{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The base removes an \(\alpha\) hydrogen to give the enolate, which attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule. The HEATING is essential: it is what eliminates water and carries the aldol on to the unsaturated aldehyde, driven by the conjugation of the new double bond with the carbonyl.

(2) PROPANOIC ACID TO 2-CHLOROPROPANOIC ACID — the HELL-VOLHARD-ZELINSKY reaction, which halogenates at the \(\alpha\) position:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(Cl)COOH}\)

The red phosphorus is essential: it converts the acid into its acyl chloride, which enolises far more readily than the acid itself, and it is the enol that chlorine attacks.

(ii) OZONOLYSIS cleaves a carbon-carbon double bond and puts an oxygen on each fragment, so identifying the fragments rebuilds the alkene.

'B' gives a POSITIVE Fehling's test, so it is an ALDEHYDE; it also gives iodoform, so it carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group. The only compound satisfying both is
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal

'C' does NOT give Fehling's, so it is a KETONE, and it gives iodoform, so it too has a methyl on the carbonyl:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), propanone

Rejoining the two carbonyl carbons by a double bond gives the alkene, and the carbon count confirms it — two plus three, and the two oxygens are not part of the original:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3{-}CH{=}C(CH_3)_2}\), 2-methylbut-2-ene, \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\)
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}C(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{Zn}/\mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \mathrm{O_3}} \mathrm{CH_3CHO} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Distinguish with a suitable chemical test :
(1) \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO}\)
(2) Ethanal and Ethanoic acid
(ii) Write the structure of oxime of acetone.
(iii) Identify A to D.
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCl_5}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2/Pd-BaSO_4}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H_3O^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ CH_3/MgBr}} \mathrm{C}\)
and \(\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{D}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Sub-part (iii) is printed as a BRANCHED two-dimensional reaction scheme: a horizontal chain CH3COOH -> A -> B -> C, with a separate arrow dropping VERTICALLY from B, labelled LiAlH4, to D. The linear transcription above splits it into a horizontal chain plus a second line 'and B --LiAlH4--> D'; that is faithful but is not what the page looks like, so the real crop should be attached. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Use TOLLENS' REAGENT. Warmed with it, BUTANAL gives a bright SILVER MIRROR, the aldehyde being oxidised to butanoic acid while silver ion is reduced to the metal; BUTANONE gives no reaction, a ketone resisting such mild oxidation.

Fehling's solution serves the same way, butanal giving a red precipitate of copper(I) oxide.

The IODOFORM test would also distinguish them, but in the OPPOSITE direction: butanone carries a \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group and gives a yellow precipitate, while butanal does not.

(2) Add SODIUM HYDROGENCARBONATE solution to each. ETHANOIC ACID gives brisk EFFERVESCENCE of carbon dioxide; ETHANAL gives none:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{NaHCO_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}\uparrow\)

Tollens' reagent works in the opposite direction here — ethanal gives the mirror, ethanoic acid nothing, being already at the acid's oxidation level.

(ii) Hydroxylamine condenses with the carbonyl group of propanone, losing water:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C}{=}\mathrm{N}{-}\mathrm{OH}\)

That is ACETONE OXIME, propan-2-one oxime.

(iii) Phosphorus pentachloride replaces the hydroxyl of the acid by chlorine:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3COCl}\), ethanoyl chloride

Hydrogen over palladium on barium sulphate is ROSENMUND'S REDUCTION, whose poisoned catalyst stops at the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), ethanal

A Grignard reagent adds a methyl group to that aldehyde, and hydrolysis gives a SECONDARY alcohol with one carbon more:
\(\mathrm{C} = (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{CHOH}\), propan-2-ol

Lithium aluminium hydride instead reduces the aldehyde to the PRIMARY alcohol, with the carbon count unchanged:
\(\mathrm{D} = \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\), ethanol

The last two steps make the contrast: a hydride reagent only REDUCES, while a Grignard reagent reduces and ADDS A CARBON, which is why one gives ethanol and the other propan-2-ol from the same aldehyde.
